# The French Revolution

## Professor Bastos's Lecture on the French Revolution. {.unnumbered}

::: {.content-hidden unless-format="html"}
{{< video https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-rXk8cJCdr8 >}}
:::

Good afternoon, everyone. Please do not feel obliged to speak Castilian Spanish on my account: *si us plau, parleu en català* during the questions. While I do not speak Catalan fluently, I take great pleasure in listening to it. Furthermore, they promised me that by the time I visited Catalonia, you would already be independent, making me the first Spanish or Galician guest speaker to visit an independent republic—yet I see you still have some homework left to do! But it will come soon enough.

Now then, I intend to speak without strict time constraints. One of the pathologies of the French Revolution was its obsession with rationalizing time and metricizing human existence on a decimal scale. I will speak for as long as the material demands, and then we will open the floor to your questions until I must catch my train. I dislike delivering closed lectures; I want you to challenge me, interrogate my arguments, and debate the historical issues raised here.

As Martín mentioned, I am not a professional historian. I make no claim to expertise where I possess none: I am a mediocre political scientist and an even worse economist! But I have always maintained a deep fascination with the French Revolution, and I believe it has been poorly handled from a libertarian perspective. History is almost universally authored by scholars who command vast archival knowledge but lack grounding in Austrian economics or libertarian political theory. Consequently, their analyses often miss the structural economic mechanisms underlying the events they describe.

Historians describe skyrocketing bread prices, the runaway inflation of the *assignats*, severe food shortages, and urban riots, yet they rarely grasp the economic laws driving those phenomena. The explanation is textbook: impose a legal price ceiling on grain amidst wartime inflation, and shortages are guaranteed! I want to offer an interpretation through a libertarian lens. And I urge any historians or students of history in this audience: please write historical works from our perspective. There is a desperate need for sound Austrian and libertarian historical scholarship.

The overarching question of this lecture is: was the French Revolution the root of all modern evil? Obviously not *all* evil. I am sharply critical of the Revolution, but it accomplished certain positive reforms. It abolished slavery, for instance—a milestone that must be credited to it, even if the clumsy execution sparked the catastrophic Haitian War and the devastation of an entire nation. It also abolished feudal class privileges. But it abolished them in reverse: under the *Ancien Régime*, the nobility enjoyed exemption from taxation. The libertarian solution would have been to extend that tax exemption to the entire population, rather than subjecting every citizen to the fiscal clutches of the State!

Why, then, am I so critical of the French Revolution?

First: it established a Republic. The Jacobins and their fellow revolutionaries were steeped in classical republican rhetoric: civic virtue, the collective common good, an enlightened citizenry, and absolute "incorruptibility"—hence [Maximilien Robespierre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maximilien_Robespierre)^[Prominent leader of the French Revolution.] was hailed as "The Incorruptible." They overthrew the monarchy in the name of an idealized republic. Was that progress?

I am a monarchist—just as Catalans were historically part of the Principality of Catalonia, and Galicians part of the Kingdom of Galicia. Why do I defend monarchy? Because historical monarchy was a comparatively civilized, orderly mode of governance. Under Louis XVI, French society was advancing through a steady civilizing process. Liberties were expanding and the nation was prospering. Consider: where did the great Enlightenment philosophers—[Voltaire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voltaire), [Rousseau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Jacques_Rousseau), [D'Holbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baron_d%27Holbach), [Montesquieu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Montesquieu), and [Diderot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Denis_Diderot)—publish their works? Were their treatises burned at the stake? Were they rotting in underground dungeons? No: they constituted the reigning intellectual elite of Paris, patronized by the aristocracy! The repressive caricature of that monarchy is largely historical mythology.

Monarchy represents an orderly, long-term political arrangement. When the Republic arrived, it immediately unleashed chronic institutional instability. In Spain, centuries of traditional monarchy witnessed virtually no military coups; governance was stable and predictable. The moment that order was shattered, politics devolved into *pronunciamientos*, military insurrections, street riots, and civil war.

In *The Civilizing Process* [@elias1939civilizing], the German sociologist [Norbert Elias](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Norbert_Elias) demonstrated that societies slowly become more peaceful, courteous, and civilized through commerce, reciprocal exchange, and customary manners. Monarchy aligns with this civilizing trajectory because its time preference is extraordinarily low: a hereditary king manages the realm as an inherited family estate to be passed down to his children, rather than plundering it during a four-year electoral cycle.

I am an anarchist—an anarcho-capitalist. Yet I maintain that traditional monarchy is far closer to anarchy than a modern democratic republic ever can be. Why? Because a monarch commands very little democratic legitimacy. When a king imposes taxes, subjects recognize him as an arbitrary ruler and resist fiercely. Historically, European monarchs rarely succeeded in levying taxes exceeding 10% of output, because subjects would revolt and burn royal tax offices. Modern democratic republics, by contrast, cloaked in the myth that "we are the government," routinely extract 50% or 60% of citizens' income with virtually no resistance!

Had the Revolution not violently interrupted that civilizing evolution, European monarchies would likely have transitioned toward peaceful, decentralized micro-states resembling modern Liechtenstein or Monaco—prosperous realms characterized by minimal state interference, robust civil liberties, and flourishing commerce. Instead, the Revolution inaugurated "aristocide": the systematic extermination of the hereditary nobility via the guillotine, clearing away the primary aristocratic buffer that historically checked the expansion of central state power.

Second: the destruction of regional autonomy and local institutions. The supreme ambition of the modern centralizing state is the eradication of intermediate associations and local authorities. The French Revolution abolished provincial *parlements*, crushed regional self-governance, and forcibly imposed standard Parisian French across the territory. In 1789, only 20% to 25% of the population spoke Parisian French as their native tongue. France was a mosaic of living languages: Basque, Catalan, Breton, Occitan, and Alsatian German. The Jacobins systematically demonized regional tongues as reactionary *patois*, eradicating them through compulsory state schooling in order to manufacture national uniformity.

To dissolve historical loyalties, the National Assembly carved France into eighty-three geometric departments. Departments were artificial administrative units drawn on maps to dilute regional identities. In the Basque Country, Basque-speaking territories were deliberately merged with Francophone districts to submerge the local culture.

This geometric mania extended everywhere. The revolutionaries instituted the metric system, decimalized time into ten-hour days and hundred-minute hours, and replaced the Gregorian calendar with a ten-day revolutionary week. In Spain, liberal admirers like [Valentín de Foronda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valentin_de_Foronda)^[Consul general in Philadelphia and Minister plenipotentiary to the United States.] proposed dividing Spain into equal squares of 500 square leagues with numbers instead of historical names!

In *Seeing Like a State* [@scott1998seeing], the political anthropologist [James C. Scott](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/James_C._Scott) explains that this standardization is never innocent: it is designed to render society "legible" to the tax collector and the conscription officer. When villagers measure grain in local customary units like *ferrados* or *ollas*, central tax extraction is difficult. Standardizing liters, kilograms, and land plots enables bureaucratic surveillance. For the same reason, the State assigns every citizen a permanent surname, a fiscal identification number, and an official street address: so that the bureaucratic apparatus can track, tax, and conscript you without friction.

Third: aggressive secularism and the manufacture of a civic religion. A centralizing state cannot tolerate an autonomous moral authority. Rulers seek to become the sole source of law and morality, redefining righteousness as statutory legality. The Catholic Church stood as an independent institutional rival, commanding its own courts, revenues, and social loyalty. The revolutionaries assaulted it mercilessly: confiscating ecclesiastical estates, enacting the Civil Constitution of the Clergy, and persecuting "refractory" priests who refused to swear allegiance to the state.

Robespierre understood that pure atheism could not inspire mass obedience. Mimicking Machiavelli's reading of Livy, he created a civic state religion: the Cult of the Supreme Being and the Cult of Reason. The painter [Jacques-Louis David](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacques-Louis_David) staged colossal secular liturgies in Notre-Dame, complete with choruses, ceremonial processions, and the planting of "Liberty Trees." The objective was replacing devotion to God with religious worship of the Republic and the Nation.

Fourth: radical egalitarianism. The Jacobin devotion to equality was so absolute that in Strasbourg they contemplated demolishing the cathedral spire because it soared higher than surrounding roofs! This egalitarian dogma birthed compulsory state education, designed to mold obedient citizens drilled in loyalty to the State. By 1796, [Gracchus Babeuf](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fran%C3%A7ois-No%C3%ABl_Babeuf) and his [Conspiracy of the Equals](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Conspiracy_of_the_Equals) pushed Jacobinism to its logical totalitarian conclusion: proto-communist abolition of all private property.

Fifth: mass warfare and universal military conscription. Perhaps the most catastrophic invention of the French Revolution was the *levée en masse*—universal conscription. As Hoffman Nickerson documented in *The Armed Horde, 1793–1939* [@nickerson1940armed], the Revolution transformed warfare from restrained dynastic conflicts between small mercenary forces into total wars between armed populations.

In the *Ancien Régime*, wars were fought by relatively small armies; civilians were largely spared, and trade often continued between belligerent nations. The Revolution converted warfare into an ideological frenzy of "citizens to arms." This democratic militarism made possible the slaughter of the Napoleonic Wars, which claimed millions of European lives, paving the ideological runway for the industrialized butcheries of the First and Second World Wars.

Furthermore, the Girondins championed the doctrine of "exporting the revolution" by force of arms. As [Claes Ryn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Claes_G._Ryn) observes in *America the Virtuous* [@ryn2003america], modern neoconservative crusades to "impose democracy" across the Middle East draw directly from the Jacobin doctrine that nations must be "forced to be free."

Sixth: economic devastation. While the Revolution began with liberal rhetoric—endorsed initially by economists like [Jean-Baptiste Say](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Baptiste_Say) and manifested in the [Le Chapelier Law](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Le_Chapelier_Law_1791) abolishing guilds—it rapidly devolved into disastrous economic interventionism. Having confiscated Church lands, the Assembly issued paper currency called *assignats*. Overissuance sparked hyperinflation; to suppress rising prices, the Jacobins passed the Law of the Maximum, imposing price ceilings on essential commodities. As [Henry Hazlitt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Henry_Hazlitt) explains in *Economics in One Lesson* [@hazlitt1952economics], price controls instantly produced catastrophic shortages and famine. The regime scapegoated merchants, executing "hoarders" and "speculators" on the guillotine to distract from its own monetary mismanagement.

Crucially, the Revolution eroded the absolute concept of private property, subordinating it to the "social function of property." Once property is stripped of its absolute character and conditioned upon collective social utility, ownership is reduced to a precarious usufruct granted at the discretion of the ruler.

Seventh: the Reign of Terror. We must distinguish fear from terror. Fear is predictable and directed: political dissidents fear a regime because their specific actions are targeted. Terror, by contrast, is arbitrary and unpredictable: anyone can be dragged to the scaffold at any moment. As Victor Hugo captured in *Ninety-Three* [@hugo1874ninetythree] and Robert Margerit in *The Reign of Terror* [@margerit1963reinado], terror was deployed deliberately to atomize society, severing mutual trust so that no collective resistance could crystallize.

Nowhere was this more horrifying than in the [War in the Vendée](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_in_the_Vend%C3%A9e) and the [Chouannerie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chouannerie). When rural populations in western France revolted to defend their local customs, priests, and autonomy, the revolutionary regime unleashed "infernal columns," slaughtering hundreds of thousands of civilians in a campaign many historians characterize as genocide.

Eighth: tyrannicide. The Revolution also recalled the ancient doctrine of tyrannicide, embodied by [Charlotte Corday](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charlotte_Corday), the young woman who assassinated the bloodthirsty Jacobin [Jean-Paul Marat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jean-Paul_Marat) in his bathtub. Inspired by Plutarch and the Hispanic scholastic tradition of Juan de Mariana, she recognized Marat as a political monster who orchestrated the September Massacres, and delivered justice when institutional remedies had perished.

I invite you to explore these historical themes from a sound libertarian perspective, and I thank you for your kind attention.

### Question: "Regarding the decimal system: wouldn't it have been natural to count on ten fingers and build the decimal standard from that?" {.unnumbered}

There are numerous mathematical bases: Babylonians used base-60, which still governs our sixty-minute hours and 360-degree circles. Roman numerals relied heavily on base-5. Modern computing operates on base-2 binary. There is nothing inherently sacred about base-10. What was tyrannical was the Jacobin determination to impose a uniform decimal grid on every facet of existence—even attempting to mandate ten-day weeks and divide the quadrant of the meridian into an abstract platinum-iridium bar in Paris to supersede all organic, localized human customs.

### Question: "How were property rights structured prior to the French Revolution?" {.unnumbered}

As [Richard Pipes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Richard_Pipes) documents in *Property and Freedom* [@pipes2000property], classical civil law recognized property as *ius utendi, fruendi, et abutendi*: the right to use, enjoy the fruits of, and even consume or dispose of an asset. If land was mine, I held sovereign jurisdiction over it. Under the modern "social function of property" inherited from the Revolution, private property is degraded to a conditional lease. The municipality tells you whether you may rent your flat on Airbnb, dictates the color of your façade, or forbids you from adding a story for your children. When "social function" governs, property rights are whatever the ruling politician decrees them to be.

### Question: "Why was female equality neglected during the Revolution, and what virtues do you find in monarchy?" {.unnumbered}

While the Jacobin constitution proclaimed universal suffrage, it explicitly restricted voting to males. Furthermore, the Revolution nationalized marriage. Previously, matrimony was a private, religious, and contractual covenant. By creating civil marriage, the State usurped the authority to define matrimonial validity, inserting the bureaucracy into private intimate life.

Regarding monarchy: a monarchy differs from a democratic republic in that the state apparatus is managed as private property rather than public property. When you own a house, you maintain the roof, protect the plumbing, and care for its long-term asset value. When you rent a flat temporarily, you exploit it with minimal regard for its enduring condition. An absolute monarch treats the realm as an inherited family estate: plundering his subjects excessively destroys his own tax base and impoverishes his dynastic heirs. An elected president or prime minister, by contrast, has only four or five years to extract maximum resources for his political coalition before vacating office.

Moreover, the apparent virtue of monarchy is its lack of democratic legitimacy. When subjects see a crowned king, they recognize an alien power and resist tax hikes. When citizens in a republic are indoctrinated with the slogan that "we are the government," their psychological defenses collapse, enabling the democratic State to levy unprecedented tax burdens.

### Question: "What do you think of the concept of the 'age of majority'?" {.unnumbered}

An age of majority that historically left young men free from peacetime conscription, compared to modern revolutionary states that declare you "mature" at eighteen precisely in order to drag you into military trenches to perish in foreign wars? That is a fictitious, bureaucratic maturity. Paper constitutions and declarations of rights do not generate genuine liberty. The great Enlightenment thinkers published and debated vigorously under monarchy without requiring modern statutory bills of rights.

### Question: "What are the advantages of centralization over regional fragmentation?" {.unnumbered}

Centralization is an unmitigated disaster for liberty; political fragmentation is the greatest engine of human freedom. The triumph of European civilization lay precisely in its political disunity: Europe was united culturally and religiously, yet divided into hundreds of competing principalities, free cities, and cantons. If a prince became tyrannical, capital and merchants simply moved twenty miles into a neighboring jurisdiction.

Consider the Dutch United Provinces: eight fiercely independent provinces, maintaining distinct laws, privileges, and currencies, yet they out-competed the greatest empires of Europe and defeated the Spanish Crown. Decentralization does not prevent integration; it fosters genuine integration. In the Middle Ages, a scholar could study anywhere from Bologna to Oxford without a passport, using a stable, honest gold currency.

Consider the [Taifas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taifa) of medieval Islamic Spain: when the central caliphate collapsed, small independent kingdoms emerged. The Taifa of Murcia issued the famous gold dinar of the [Wolf King](https://es.wikipedia.org/wiki/Muh%C3%A1mmad_ibn_Mardan%C3%ADs), which became the premier trade currency of the Mediterranean because a small state cannot afford to debase its currency.

### Question: "Are large states more militarily effective than small states?" {.unnumbered}

Centralized imperial states are often remarkably fragile. A few hundred Spanish conquistadors toppled the vast Inca and Aztec empires in a matter of weeks, because once the supreme emperor was captured, the entire centralized hierarchy surrendered. Conversely, decentralized, stateless peoples—such as the Comanches, the Mapuches of Chile, or the Germanic tribes against Rome—resisted conquest for centuries because there was no central capital to seize. Decentralized societies are infinitely more resilient.

### Question: "Is North Korea a monarchy?" {.unnumbered}

North Korea is not a genuine monarchy; it is a totalitarian democratic republic. Even though power passes dynastically, the regime does not derive its legitimacy from historical bloodline primogeniture as a private proprietary domain, but from claiming to embody the "popular democratic will" and the revolutionary party.

### Question: "How is private property protected in an anarchist society?" {.unnumbered}

Private property is already protected privately every day: through private title registries, security companies, commercial arbitration, and neighborhood watch associations. When you visit a private shopping mall or gated condominium, security is maintained entirely by private personnel. The debate between minarchists and anarcho-capitalists is not whether private defense is operationally feasible—it clearly is—but whether coercive state monopolies over defense and justice possess any ethical legitimacy. In our view, they possess none.
